sources_considered.why: Primary experimental evidence that AI-generated answers can receive ordinary university credit undetected.
Full paper verifies the experiment's summer 2023 timing and explains that actual student cheating prevalence was not measured.
Available before the evaluation date and materially qualifies broad deterioration claims; pooled observation period extends beyond the post.
Reports an association between detector-classified AI use and lower exam results. Detector classification and non-random use prevent treating that association as decisive causal evidence.
Measures adoption and perceptions rather than causal learning loss or actual assessment invalidity.

evidence_items.publisher: PLOS ONE, abstract hosted by PubMed
evidence_items.explanation: The blind insertion of AI-written answers establishes a concrete assessment-integrity problem caused by using GenAI. It supports that component of the claim, but does not measure widespread student cheating or learning loss.

A large US university study finds limited evidence of broad grade and satisfaction deterioration, qualifying the general harm claim. Its pooled data extend through fall 2025, and grades and satisfaction are not direct measures of learning, so it is context rather than decisive target-period counterevidence.

unresolved_gaps: The experiment does not establish how frequently students actually outsourced assessed work.
No cited study establishes the scale of causal learning losses across universities by the post date.
The large institutional comparison does not isolate the claimed period or directly measure independent learning.
The wording leaves unresolved whether assessment vulnerability alone satisfies huge problem.
